title: Unconditional cash transfers can shift parental investment through money or time differently across racialized groups
source_unit: U.S. families in a large-scale multisite randomized unconditional-cash-transfer study, analyzed by race and ethnicity

observations.period: Monthly unconditional cash-transfer intervention; NBER Working Paper issued May 2025

denominator.unit: randomized study frame; abstract does not state one pooled respondent denominator

net_household_income_earnings_expenditur.value: similar effects across racial and ethnic groups
net_household_income_earnings_expenditur.unit: reported treatment pattern for net household income, earnings, and household expenditures

latino_child_focused_expenditures.value: increased by an amount equivalent to nearly one-third of the cash transfer

latino_maternal_work_and_child_time.value: no effect on maternal employment or time spent with children

black_maternal_work_hours.unit: reported treatment direction for maternal work hours

black_child_early_learning_time.unit: reported treatment direction for time spent with children on early-learning activities

income_source_signal.value: marginal propensity to consume child-specific goods differed by income source: higher from government income than maternal income among Latino families, with the opposite pattern among Black families

observations.method: NBER Working Paper 33737 analyzes a large-scale, multisite U.S. randomized study of monthly unconditional cash transfers and estimates heterogeneous effects on monetary and time investments in children by race and ethnicity.
observations.uncertainty: This record retains the official abstract-level treatment patterns rather than reproduced coefficients, sample construction, treatment amount, compliance, or full robustness results. Race and ethnicity are analytic subgroup dimensions, not biological mechanisms; the abstract does not identify the household's complete care substitution, stress, political response, or later child outcome.
observations.subgroup: Families analyzed as Latino and Black subgroups in the randomized study; the abstract also notes initial differences in family structure, government-benefit receipt, and employment.
observations.counterinterpretation: Similar effects on total income and expenditures can coexist with different time and child-investment responses. A fall in maternal work hours may represent reallocation toward care, but the abstract does not establish whether it reflects schedule control, reduced labor demand, stress, childcare constraints, or a durable employment change.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI and working-paper metadata identify the study and authors.

boundary: This is a randomized U.S. transfer-to-parental-investment result with heterogeneous subgroup pathways, not a universal cash-transfer effect or a complete household-welfare, care-quality, labor-market, trust, or political-action estimate.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official NBER Working Paper 33737 page downloaded and hashed; title, date, randomized-study design, subgroup treatment patterns, and source-of-income qualification checked against the abstract.
